title: Legal Departments Show Growing AI Adoption But Implementation Challenges Remain, New Survey Finds
author: Bob Ambrogi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that adoption alone does not deliver organisational value and materially extends it with survey evidence from in-house legal departments: practical use is expanding, especially in contracts and research, while infrastructure, expertise, trust, training, governance and ROI measurement remain underdeveloped. Its evidence is geographically concentrated and descriptive rather than causal, but directly reinforces the need for selective deployment and operating-model readiness.
qs: While the findings indicate that AI in legal departments is moving beyond experimental phases toward practical implementation, significant work remains in developing the infrastructure and expertise needed for mature AI adoption.

As the legal profession continues to grapple with AI integration, this data suggests that while early adoption is promising, success will depend heavily on addressing trust, training, and governance challenges that currently limit broader deployment.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that enthusiasm and perceived efficiency do not establish investment value. It reports weak KPI and spending visibility alongside persistent trust and privacy barriers, and its strong preference for lawyer-controlled assistance over autonomy reinforces the cluster’s bounded, implementation-focused account.
qs: Only 7% of departments use specific KPIs to track AI value, and 40% of respondents remain “not sure yet” whether their AI tools are worth the investment.
Sixty percent of respondents cited “lack of trust or quality in AI outputs” as their top implementation challenge, followed closely by data privacy concerns (57%).

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by documenting substantial in-house AI adoption and planned expansion from foundational tasks into legal operations and workflow automation, while identifying trust, privacy and measurement as continuing organisational barriers. It provides survey evidence of adoption and intentions, not proof of completed market-wide transformation or captured cost gains.
qs: “The results show a clear trend: legal departments are starting with foundational AI applications like contract drafting and legal research, but are preparing to expand their AI usage into broader operational areas,” the report states.
However, significant barriers around trust, data privacy, and measurement persist as the legal profession navigates this technological shift.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source indirectly supports the cluster’s preference for lawyer-supervised, governed AI use: even in-house legal departments identify trust, reliability, privacy and skills barriers, and overwhelmingly favour AI suggesting options while lawyers retain control. It does not directly assess unrepresented users, access-to-justice outcomes or the downward transfer of risk, so its support is contextual rather than comprehensive.
qs: Sixty percent of respondents cited “lack of trust or quality in AI outputs” as their top implementation challenge, followed closely by data privacy concerns (57%).
When it comes to decision-making, 66% favor AI playing a supporting role by suggesting options while keeping lawyers in control, with just 1% supporting full AI autonomy in legal decisions.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that legal AI is being adopted for bounded tasks and workflow automation, while mature deployment depends on user expertise, training, trust, governance and organisational infrastructure. It provides survey evidence on adoption and readiness gaps but does not materially assess verification burdens, apprenticeship risks or lawyer replacement.
qs: While the findings indicate that AI in legal departments is moving beyond experimental phases toward practical implementation, significant work remains in developing the infrastructure and expertise needed for mature AI adoption.

As the legal profession continues to grapple with AI integration, this data suggests that while early adoption is promising, success will depend heavily on addressing trust, training, and governance challenges that currently limit broader deployment.

kp.k: Survey establishes early, predominantly Canadian in-house adoption benchmark
kp.d: Bob Ambrogi's 5 June 2025 article reports findings from Counselwell and Spellbook's inaugural AI in Legal Departments: 2025 Benchmarking Report. It surveyed 256 in-house legal professionals across North America; 90% were in-house lawyers, 86.8% were based in Canada and 10.5% in the United States. Among surveyed teams, 38% already used AI tools and another 50% were actively exploring implementation.
qs: The inaugural *AI in Legal Departments: 2025 Benchmarking Report*, published this week by Counselwell and Spellbook, surveyed 256 in-house legal professionals across North America to understand current AI adoption patterns and future expectations.
with 38% of surveyed teams already using AI tools and another 50% actively exploring implementation.
with the majority (86.8%) based in Canada and 10.5% in the United States.

kp.k: Contract work leads current use; operational expansion is anticipated
kp.d: Among AI users, 64% used tools for contract drafting, review and analysis, 49% for legal research and 38% for document translation. Over the next 1-2 years, 32% planned to adopt legal operations and workflow automation tools, while 28% were considering document automation. The report interprets this as movement from foundational applications toward broader operational use; the expansion figures describe intentions rather than completed adoption.
qs: Sixty-four percent of AI users employ tools for contract drafting, review, and analysis, followed by legal research (49%) and document translation (38%).

Looking ahead, respondents expect significant expansion into operational areas over the next 1-2 years, with 32% planning to adopt legal operations and workflow automation tools and 28% considering document automation.

kp.k: ChatGPT leads adoption; users report frequent, effective use
kp.d: Among AI-adopting respondents, reported platform usage was 74% for ChatGPT, 40% for Microsoft Copilot, 22% for Spellbook, 17% for Gemini and 11% for Claude. Users' effectiveness assessments were overwhelmingly positive: 63% rated tools somewhat effective and 34% highly effective, totaling 97%. Among active users, 68% used AI daily or weekly. These are reported usage and perceptions, not measured legal-output performance.
qs: ChatGPT dominates, with 74% usage among AI-adopting respondents.
Microsoft Copilot follows at 40%, while legal-specific tools such as Spellbook capture 22% adoption.
Rounding out the top platforms are tools such as Gemini (17%) and Claude (11%).
Nearly universal satisfaction marks early AI implementations, with 97% of users reporting their tools are somewhat (63%) or highly (34%) effective.
Among active users, 68% engage with AI tools daily or weekly, suggesting these technologies are becoming integral to legal workflows.

kp.k: Trust and privacy outweigh cost and integration barriers
kp.d: Despite positive effectiveness ratings among users, 60% of respondents identified lack of trust or quality in AI outputs as their top implementation challenge, and 57% cited data privacy concerns. These exceeded reported cost barriers at 33% and system integration issues at 36%. The findings concern implementation concerns rather than measured error rates.
qs: Sixty percent of respondents cited “lack of trust or quality in AI outputs” as their top implementation challenge, followed closely by data privacy concerns (57%).
These concerns far outweighed traditional barriers like cost (33%) or system integration issues (36%).

kp.k: Reported efficiency gains coexist with weak ROI measurement
kp.d: Although 83% of users cited increased efficiency as AI's primary benefit, only 7% of departments used specific KPIs to track its value. Forty percent of respondents remained unsure whether tools justified their investment. The article therefore distinguishes perceived benefits from underdeveloped formal return-on-investment measurement.
qs: While 83% of users cite increased efficiency as the primary benefit of AI adoption, formal measurement of return on investment remains underdeveloped.
Only 7% of departments use specific KPIs to track AI value, and 40% of respondents remain “not sure yet” whether their AI tools are worth the investment.

kp.d: The article characterizes monthly AI spending as modest for most departments: 26% spent under $100 per month and only 9% more than $2,000 monthly. However, 44% of respondents did not know their department's spending, which the author interprets as suggesting a need to improve budget tracking.
qs: Monthly spending on AI tools remains modest for most departments, with 26% spending under $100 per month and only 9% spending more than $2,000 monthly.
However, 44% of respondents didn’t know their department’s AI spending, suggesting budget tracking may also need refinement.

kp.k: Respondents expect task automation and favor lawyer-controlled decisions
kp.d: Expectations leaned toward augmentation: 64% believed AI would automate some tasks without replacing lawyers, 26% expected more fundamental changes in how in-house lawyers operate, and 10% anticipated minimal impact. Separately, 66% favored AI suggesting options while lawyers retained control, whereas only 1% supported full AI autonomy in legal decisions. These are expectations and preferences, not observed employment or decision-making outcomes.
qs: Sixty-four percent believe AI will automate some tasks without replacing lawyers, while 26% expect more fundamental changes to how in-house lawyers operate.
Only 10% anticipate minimal impact.
When it comes to decision-making, 66% favor AI playing a supporting role by suggesting options while keeping lawyers in control, with just 1% supporting full AI autonomy in legal decisions.

kp.k: AI literacy and organizational policies remain uneven
kp.d: Fifty-nine percent described themselves as somewhat familiar with AI tools, but only 24% felt they strongly understood AI fundamentals and implications for legal work. Organizational policy development also varied: 48% had AI policies or guidelines, 26% were developing them and 21% lacked them entirely. Respondents identified training, accuracy and reliability, and clearer regulatory guidance as missing elements of the legal AI discussion; one respondent specifically advocated prompting training.
qs: While 59% of respondents describe themselves as “somewhat familiar” with AI tools, only 24% feel they have strong understanding of AI fundamentals and implications for legal work.
While 48% of organizations have implemented AI policies or guidelines, 26% are still developing them and 21% lack policies entirely.

When asked what’s missing from the AI discussion in legal, respondents highlighted three key areas: the need for better training and skill development, concerns about AI accuracy and reliability, and the lack of clear regulatory guidelines.

“Lawyers need to be trained on AI prompting to get the full value from GenAI tools. If you don’t ask the right questions, you will never get the right answers,” one respondent noted, reflecting broader calls for enhanced AI literacy among legal professionals.

kp.k: Technology-company legal departments are overrepresented among AI users
kp.d: The survey found that 36% of AI-using respondents worked in the technology sector, compared with technology companies accounting for 23% of all survey participants. The article presents this difference as evidence that technology-company legal departments are leading adoption.
qs: The survey found that legal departments at technology companies are leading the adoption wave, with 36% of AI-using respondents working in the tech sector, despite tech companies representing only 23% of all survey participants.

kp.k: Mature deployment depends on training, trust and governance
kp.d: The report presents itself as an early benchmark and highlights improved training, clearer ROI frameworks and stronger organizational policies as opportunities. Ambrogi concludes that adoption is moving beyond experimentation toward practical implementation, but that successful broader deployment depends on addressing trust, training and governance and developing supporting infrastructure and expertise. This is the article's synthesis and conditional outlook rather than a separately measured survey outcome.
qs: The report positions itself as “a valuable early benchmark for in-house legal teams navigating the rapidly evolving legal AI ecosystem” while highlighting opportunities for improved training, clearer ROI frameworks, and stronger organizational policies.

As the legal profession continues to grapple with AI integration, this data suggests that while early adoption is promising, success will depend heavily on addressing trust, training, and governance challenges that currently limit broader deployment.

While the findings indicate that AI in legal departments is moving beyond experimental phases toward practical implementation, significant work remains in developing the infrastructure and expertise needed for mature AI adoption.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi reports expanding practical AI use in corporate legal departments, concentrated initially in contracts and research, with respondents anticipating broader operational use and predominantly lawyer-controlled task automation.
pts.d: Reporting the Counselwell and Spellbook survey, Ambrogi states that 38% of surveyed teams already use AI and 50% are exploring implementation. Among AI users, 64% use it for contract drafting, review and analysis, 49% for legal research and 38% for translation. ChatGPT leads reported platform use at 74%, followed by Microsoft Copilot at 40% and Spellbook at 22%. Respondents anticipate expansion into legal operations and workflow automation (32%) and document automation (28%). Reported benefits and effectiveness are substantial: 83% of users cite efficiency as the primary benefit, 97% describe tools as somewhat or highly effective, and 68% use them daily or weekly. These are reported perceptions and use patterns, not measured productivity gains. Regarding future roles, 64% expect automation of some tasks without lawyer replacement, 26% expect more fundamental changes to in-house practice, and 10% expect minimal impact. Separately, 66% prefer AI to suggest options while lawyers retain control, versus 1% favoring full autonomy; these are preferences rather than predictions. Ambrogi concludes that adoption is moving toward practical implementation but that trust, training and governance constrain broader deployment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on an inaugural survey of 256 predominantly Canadian in-house legal professionals; benefits, expectations and barriers are respondent reports rather than independently measured outcomes.
pts.d: Ambrogi's evidence source is the AI in Legal Departments: 2025 Benchmarking Report, published by Counselwell and Spellbook. Ninety percent of respondents were in-house lawyers; 86.8% were based in Canada and 10.5% in the United States. Adoption, tool use, satisfaction, efficiency, spending and future expectations are reported survey results. The article supplies no longitudinal comparison to quantify adoption growth and no independently measured time savings or financial returns. It explicitly reports limited formal measurement: only 7% of departments use specific KPIs to track AI value, and 40% of respondents are unsure whether the investment is worthwhile. Spending visibility is also limited, with 44% not knowing their department's AI expenditure. Evidence of implementation constraints includes reported concerns about output trust or quality (60%) and privacy (57%), limited strong AI understanding (24%), and uneven organizational policies. A quoted anonymous respondent advocates prompting training; that statement is a respondent's view, not a demonstrated training outcome.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article presents a June 2025 adoption snapshot, a one-to-two-year operational expansion horizon, and broader role-change expectations without a specified deadline.
pts.d: Published on 5 June 2025, the article describes the newly released survey as an early benchmark; exact fieldwork dates are not supplied. The explicit forecast window is the next one to two years for legal operations, workflow automation and document automation. Predictions about task automation and changes to in-house roles have no specific timeframe. Ambrogi conditions mature, broader deployment on addressing output trust and reliability, data privacy, training, governance and measurement. Sixty percent report trust or quality as a top implementation challenge, 57% report privacy concerns, 36% integration issues and 33% cost. Only 24% report strong understanding of AI fundamentals and implications; 48% of organizations have policies or guidelines, 26% are developing them and 21% lack them. High effectiveness ratings apply to existing users, not all departments, and do not establish mature implementation or financial value.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source primarily concerns corporate in-house lawyers and their departments, especially technology-sector teams, rather than law firms or the public.
pts.d: The affected population is the buyer side of legal services: corporate legal departments and their lawyers, represented here mainly by Canadian respondents. AI is reported to assist their contract work, research and translation, with anticipated expansion into departmental workflows and document automation. Respondents predominantly envisage lawyers retaining decision-making control while tasks are automated, alongside training needs and changes in working practices. Organizations face policy, privacy, integration, budgeting and ROI-tracking demands. Technology-company departments are disproportionately represented among adopters: technology accounts for 36% of AI-using respondents but 23% of all participants. The article does not offer concrete findings about law-firm staffing, outside-counsel demand, legal-service prices, lawyer job losses or access to justice.
